# Evidence behind the ranking

Every number here is recomputed from
`.claude/skills/amg-llm-bench/data/*.yaml` by
`.claude/skills/amg-llm-bench/scripts/rank_llms.py`; none is written
by hand. It is the same evidence the page `results/frontiers.html`
shows, in a form that greps and diffs.

## How to judge this

Capability per cost is the ranking key, and it is the mean of three
equal thirds, each min-max scaled over the models present: list-price
cheapness (0.3334), cost-per-task cheapness (0.3333) and raw
capability (0.3333). A model has to earn its place on all three; no
single axis can carry it. The name is a name, not a sum you can do:
the three thirds are averaged, never divided one by another. The two
cost thirds are scaled in log space, because price spans three orders
of magnitude here.

Nothing here is filled in. A variant is scored on the boards it was
itself measured on at its own reasoning effort and on no others: no
board is carried over from another effort, another model or a ratio,
and a variant no same-source cost ratio reaches has no cost per task
rather than a guessed one. Its capability per cost is then the two
thirds it has, renormalised, and its row says price-only.

The scores come from one fit per group over exactly the cells that
exist. Every board is put on a 0-100 scale by its own median and
inter-quartile range — the median lands on 50 and 3 of those ranges
either side of it reach the ends, so a board the pool is near-flat on
uses a third of the scale rather than all of it. Then one
least-squares fit reads every score in the group at once as two
numbers added together: a level for the board and an ability for the
variant, each cell weighted by its board's weight. The board level
absorbs how hard or how generous a board is; the ability that is left
is the raw capability printed here. Variants that share boards are
compared through them, and variants that do not are compared through
the chain that connects them — so a model measured on a group's easy
half no longer outranks one measured on its hard half.

One fit cannot compare two reasoning efforts of one model that were
run on different boards: it has a level per board and an ability per
row and no term for the two together, so a weakness the whole model
shares on the boards only one effort was run on is charged to that
effort alone. So within a model the best-measured effort keeps the
fit's ability and every other effort is placed at that ability plus
the two rows' weighted mean gap on the boards both were measured on.
Under 1 shared boards there is no gap worth reading and the row keeps
the fit's own answer, saying so in its status.

A variant on fewer than 3 of a group's boards is left out of that
group's fit, chart and table and named under it instead. Measured
boards and evidence coverage say how much of the group a row was run
on, and the ability band is the standard error the fit puts on it.

Read a sparse row as optimistic. Which boards a lab publishes is not
a coin toss: a model is entered where it does well, so across this
catalogue a row's coverage and its score rise together. The fit
cannot correct for that, because the missing cells are missing, so it
is left visible instead — a row on few boards with a wide band is the
best of what was published, not the average of what was run.

Every plotted row sets the per-board scales, but a row may only sit
on a frontier once it carries enough of the group's benchmark weight.
One that is under that bar says too thin for the frontier in its
status, is drawn as a hollow dashed dot, and is listed among the
least-measured models in its group.

Columns, in plain words:

- **capability per cost** — how good the model is, set against what
  it costs: the mean of three equal thirds, each min-max scaled over
  the plotted variants.
- **raw capability (0-100)** — how well the model suits this group's
  work, from the group's own benchmark weights.
- **preference** — the same fit run over this group's Arena boards
  alone — blind human votes; `-` where the row carries no Arena board
  here at all. The raw capability is the mean of the pillar columns.
- **capability** — the same fit over the group's Artificial Analysis
  boards alone. A wide gap between the two pillar columns is a
  finding about the model, not an error.
- **effective cost (x reference)** — the geometric mean of relative
  list price and relative cost per task, as a multiple of the
  reference model.
- **evidence coverage** — the share of the group's benchmark weight
  this variant was measured on, at its own reasoning effort. Nothing
  else is behind the row: an unmeasured board is left out, not filled
  in.
- **measured boards** — how many of the group's boards this variant
  has a measured row on, out of how many the group weighs.
- **ability band** — the standard error of this row's ability in the
  least-squares fit: how far the raw capability could move on the
  evidence behind it. It narrows with boards measured, never with
  boards borrowed.

Status words:

- **on frontier** — nothing is both cheaper and a better fit.
- **off frontier** — something else is cheaper and fits better at
  once.
- **too thin for the frontier** — this row was not itself measured on
  enough of the group to be allowed on the frontier, and the status
  says which bar it fell under: the boards of its own it was run on,
  the share of the group's weight behind it, or both. Nothing is
  inherited — an effort placed against a better-measured sibling is
  judged on what was run at its own effort. It is still scored,
  ranked, plotted and listed among the least-measured models; a row
  nobody has really measured simply cannot set the line the rest of
  the page is read against.
- **price-only, no cost-per-task data** — no same-source ratio
  reaches this model, so it has no cost per task at all. Nothing is
  invented for it: its capability per cost is the list-price and
  raw-capability thirds alone, and its effective cost on the chart is
  its list price.
- **no cost-per-task data at this reasoning effort** — the model is
  priced per task but nobody published a cost multiplier for this
  effort, and the default effort's cost is not this effort's cost.
  The row is treated as having none.
- **pillar missing** — nobody measured this row on any board of that
  pillar, so the column is blank and the raw capability is the pillar
  that remains — which means a different thing from a mean over both,
  and says so. A row missing a pillar is not ranked at all unless
  another effort of the same model carries it.
- **effort cost measured** — a published run priced this model at
  this reasoning effort against another effort of itself, so the cost
  on this row is the effort's own cost.
- **placed relative to** — this row is an effort variant of a model
  whose best-measured variant sits on more boards, so each of its
  pillars is that variant's pillar plus the weighted mean gap between
  the two on the boards of that pillar both were measured on. A
  pillar they share no board in keeps the anchor's value: a lead on
  Arena is a statement about preference and about nothing else. A
  global fit has no model-by-board term, so a family-wide weakness on
  the boards only one variant was run on would otherwise be charged
  to that variant alone.
- **no board shared with** — this effort variant and its family's
  best-measured variant were never run on the same board, so there is
  no distance between the two to read. It keeps whatever the group's
  own fit gave it, and gets no number at all if the fit never reached
  it.
- **free listing exists** — the same model also has a free listing on
  the same id, with a :free suffix. That lane is throttled and
  temporary, so the ranking still prices the model at its paid list
  price.

### Where this is weakest

- coding-experiments: Arena's two agentic boards are the only human
  read of agent behaviour anywhere in this file, and they cover a
  fraction of the pool; until that widens the preference half here
  leans on the WebDev and coding Elos, which are votes about text.
  Nothing in the capability half scores a patch against a real
  repository's own test suite any more — SWE-bench went with the
  hand-transcribed boards — so what is left reads terminal and tool
  behaviour instead. A reproducible SWE-bench capture is the single
  biggest thing this group is missing.

- research-reasoning: Nothing here reads retrieval as a re-run task:
  the search boards that exist run on a handful of models each, which
  is an anecdote wearing a board's clothes, so search is read through
  Arena's search Elo alone. GPQA is close to saturated across the
  models anyone is actually choosing between, and CritPt reads one
  discipline. Nothing here measures whether a hypothesis was any
  good, which is the thing the step is for; the boards measure
  whether the model knows things and can find things.

- scientific-writing: No benchmark measuring scientific or academic
  paper writing covers this pool, so the capability half is
  long-context reasoning and constraint-following standing in for
  prose quality and one document-production board standing in for the
  artifact. Nothing in the group measures claim accuracy against a
  source, citation faithfulness or revision to reviewer comments.
  Read it as general writing preference held to a brief until such a
  board exists. `aa_aabriefcasetimepertask` was considered for this
  half and left out: it is a duration, not a quality, and a model
  that is fast at a briefcase task is not thereby better at writing a
  paper.

- review-judging: Judging is the step with the least direct evidence
  anywhere in this file: no board here scores a review against what a
  conference's own reviewers said. The Omniscience Index is the
  closest thing to "would it notice the claim is wrong", because it
  scores confident error negative rather than ignoring it. Until a
  review board exists this group is a proxy stack, and the `pillar
  missing` marks on thin rows are the honest part of it.

- general: A union is a stand-in for a measurement nobody has taken:
  no board anywhere in this file scores whether a plan was a good
  plan, and the steps here are the cheapest in the pipeline and the
  ones every later step inherits. The half shares the other groups
  gave their thinnest boards are dropped here — fourteen capability
  boards at one fourteenth each already hold any one of them to under
  4% of the group — so a thin board moves this group only through the
  rows that have it. Read the ordering as "good at everything", which
  is what a planning step asks for and also the vaguest thing this
  file can say.

- On no preference board at all, so that pillar is unmeasured for
  them rather than zero and what they are scored on is the pillar
  that remains: 97 rows.

- On no capability board at all, so that pillar is unmeasured for
  them rather than zero and what they are scored on is the pillar
  that remains: 80 rows.

- Effort multipliers were published for these models only, so effort
  is priced for them and unpriced everywhere else: Claude Fable 5.1,
  Claude Opus 5, Claude Sonnet 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra.

- Two runs that priced the same pair land a median of 2.53x apart
  (worst 5.84x, across 12 models). Treat that as the noise floor: a
  cost difference smaller than it means nothing.

## Where the fit disagrees with the overlap

Every pair of scored variants sharing at least 3 boards, asking
whether the fit ordered them the same way those shared boards do. A
pair can disagree honestly: the fit reads a row against the whole
group through every chain that reaches it, while the shared-board gap
reads two rows against each other alone. A wide disagreement is still
worth seeing, because it is the fit saying something the two rows'
own overlap does not.

### coding-experiments

2921 of 3224 overlapping pairs agree (90.6%); the 303 that do not are
listed here, widest contradiction first. `fit` is the gap the fit put
between the two rows, `shared` their mean gap on the boards both were
measured on, both read as the first row minus the second.

## Cost per task evidence

A ratio row relates two models measured on the same tasks in the same
published run, so nothing here crosses sources. The chaining happens
in the ranker, which solves the whole graph at once in log space with
deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash pinned at 1.00 — which is why a fitted
number matches no single source exactly.

### Effort multipliers

Effort is a cost dial, not a value one: one harness has Opus 5
solving fewer tasks at xhigh than at high while costing more. These
price the dial and never move a raw-capability score. They exist for
these models only: every other model split by effort has no cost per
task at any effort but its default, because the default's cost is not
that effort's cost and is not borrowed for it. Those rows say `no
cost-per-task data at this reasoning effort` in their status and are
placed on their list price alone.

Across the 12 models two or more runs both priced, the same pair
comes out a median of 2.53x apart and at worst 5.84x apart. That is
the noise floor under this whole axis: a cost gap smaller than it is
not evidence.

## Price evidence

List prices in $/M tokens, discounts deliberately ignored: a launch
promotion or one cheap endpoint lapses, and the ladder should not
reshuffle when it does. The blended proxy is (input + w*output)/(1 +
w), and **w is measured per task group** from the output-to-input
ratio of that group's own steps in
`.claude/skills/amg-llm-bench/data/pipeline_steps.yaml`. The table
below is the pool-wide fallback at w = 3, which is assumed and which
only a group with no measured steps reads; the blended column is that
fallback and the ranking is not.


| task group | output per input | basis |
|---|---|---|
| coding-experiments | 0.2365 | measured |
| research-reasoning | 0.1264 | measured |
| scientific-writing | 0.2127 | measured |
| review-judging | 0.0536 | measured |
| general | 0.0860 | measured |

Every one of them is far under one: agentic traffic reads far more
than it writes once the prompt, the tool results and the cache reads
are counted, so a price axis that weights output above input is
ranking on a shape the runs do not have.

### Qwen 3.7 Flash

`qwen/qwen3.7-flash`.

Rejected — teaser price, 8.88% tool errors. Vision-first model; the
$0.03/$0.13 headline is a sub-32k-prompt teaser (>=32k is
$0.10/$0.40, >=256k is $0.20/$0.80, and an agentic subagent always
lives above 32k); 8.88% tool-call error rate, about one failure in
eleven calls; zero published coding benchmarks (benchlm: "0 of 439",
unranked); single provider, no fallback.

No benchmark score is recorded for it at all.

No same-source cost ratio reaches this model.
